743.title: Let them come
743.hook: Jews sit shiva; some Muslim families receive mourners for three days: grief is meant to be accompanied
743.howItsDone: Jewish mourners sit shiva at home while the community visits and brings food, and in some Muslim families relatives and neighbors receive visitors and send meals for three days after a death.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Kristin Neff, and her self-compassion break. Your line was others feel this too.

A casserole dish on a doorstep, covered in foil, with a note taped to the lid. By evening there's another. Then a bag of bagels, a tray of fruit, somebody's aunt at the door with a pot of soup. On some streets, when there's been a death, the food starts arriving before anyone asks for it. And for the family inside, the hard part may not be cooking at all. It's opening the door. In more than one tradition, grief is meant to have company, not a quiet house.
screen: `A DISH ON THE DOORSTEP.` → `THE HARD PART: OPENING THE DOOR.` → `GRIEF IS MEANT TO HAVE COMPANY.`

segments.voice: First, the seven days. In Jewish tradition, after a burial, the close family sits shiva. They stay home, and the community comes to them. The Bible already knows a seven-day mourning: when Jacob dies, Genesis says of his son Joseph, "he made a mourning for his father seven days." Some families leave the front door unlocked during shiva, so visitors can let themselves in and the mourners don't have to get up. Second, the first meal. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, says the first meal after the burial should come from someone else's hands, not the mourner's own kitchen. Neighbors cook. The mourner's job is to eat. Third, the same instinct in another house. A hadith tells of the day news came that a man named Ja'far had died. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told the people to prepare food for Ja'far's family, because something had come to them that would keep them busy. It's in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. In some Muslim families today, relatives and neighbors receive visitors and bring meals for three days. Fourth, the other side of the door. Every one of these customs needs two people. Someone carries the soup up the path. Someone else has to open the door and take it. For a person who is used to being the helper, that second job can feel like the harder one. In these traditions, saying yes to the casserole isn't a failure at grieving. It is part of how grieving is done. The visitors come. The mourner lets them.
screen: `SEVEN DAYS AT HOME.` · `THE FIRST MEAL FROM OTHER HANDS.` · `FOOD FOR JA'FAR'S FAMILY.` · `SOMEONE HAS TO OPEN THE DOOR.` · then, large: `LET THEM COME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has offered help you waved away, or someone who would come if you asked. Let the door open in your mind, let them stand there with whatever they're carrying, and notice what happens when you imagine saying yes; if something tightens, breathe there. If you pray, you can bring that person to God by name, and then simply breathe, as someone who is allowed to be cared for.
Shiva, the week a Jewish family sits at home after a burial while the community comes to them. Today's word.
Your line: someone else's hands. Even a small yes, a ride or a coffee, counts. That's day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: One small mercy
744.hook: on a bad day, look for one small mercy
744.howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers return to Lamentations 3:22–23, 'they are new every morning', on hard days, and some people keep a nightly habit of naming one good thing from the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shiva: the community comes, and the mourner lets them. Your line was someone else's hands.

The alarm didn't go off. The train sat in a tunnel, going nowhere. There was a hard email before lunch, and a call from the clinic that ended with, we'll need to run more tests. Then, on the walk home, a stranger held the door at the corner shop, and there was one of the good rolls left, still warm. Small. Nearly nothing. It didn't fix the day. But it was there. An old book of grief has a line about exactly that, set right in the middle of its sorrow.
screen: `A DAY GOING WRONG.` → `ONE WARM ROLL.` → `A LINE IN A BOOK OF GRIEF.`

segments.voice: First, where the line lives. Lamentations is a book of poems over a ruined city. It is full of anguish. In the third chapter the poet says, "thou hast removed my soul far off from peace: I forgat prosperity." He has forgotten what good even feels like. Second, the turn. A few verses later, nothing outside has changed. The city is still in ruins. But he writes, "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." And then: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning." Notice the verb. He recalls. He doesn't deny the ruins; he turns his attention, on purpose, to something else that is also true. Third, the word. The Hebrew behind mercies is hesed. English Bibles translate it in different ways: mercy, kindness, lovingkindness. Jews and Christians read these lines as being about God's faithfulness. Someone with no faith in God can still borrow the move underneath: recall one thing that was kind today. Fourth, why small. This is not a silver lining. Last week, the line was growth isn't required, and that still stands. A small mercy doesn't explain the bad day or make it worth it. It doesn't cancel the test results. It just sits next to them: a warm roll, a held door, a text from a friend. The poet in Lamentations doesn't stop lamenting after this verse. The book goes on grieving. He has simply found one thing to hold while it does.
screen: `A BOOK OF POEMS OVER RUINS.` · `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` · `HESED: MERCY, KINDNESS.` · `NOT A SILVER LINING.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL MERCY.`

segments.voice: Let today play back for a moment, hard parts included, without arguing with them. Then look for one small mercy, small enough to miss: a kind word, hot water, a song in a shop, a minute when nothing hurt, and stay with it. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words, or with the line from Lamentations, they are new every morning, then breathe beside it.
Hesed, the Hebrew word behind mercies in Lamentations: God's mercies, new every morning, recalled on purpose inside the ruin. Today's word.
Your line: they are new every morning. A mercy doesn't have to be big to be real. Day seven hundred forty-four, done.

745.title: The wounded healer
745.hook: people who have suffered sometimes become healers, an old idea found in myths and in modern care alike
745.howItsDone: Some recovery groups and peer support programs pair people who have come through an illness, addiction or loss with those newly facing it, and some Christians read 2 Corinthians 1:4 as a call to pass on the comfort they have received.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hesed, and one small mercy beside a hard day. Your line was they are new every morning.

In Greek myth there's a centaur named Chiron, half man, half horse, who lives in a cave on a mountain and teaches young heroes. He knows herbs, music and medicine. In some tellings he teaches healing to Asclepius, who becomes the god of medicine. And Chiron carries a wound of his own: an arrow, poisoned, that struck him by accident. He is immortal, so he cannot die of it. And it will not heal. That strange picture has followed people a long way, into churches and clinics. It has a name.
screen: `A CENTAUR WHO TEACHES HEALING.` → `A WOUND THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `IT HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the myth. Chiron's wound doesn't stop his work. In the story, it sits right beside it. Much later, the psychiatrist Carl Jung wrote of the wounded physician: the idea that a healer's own hurt can be part of what lets them understand a patient's. Writers after him tied that phrase to Chiron. Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, puts the same idea in Christian terms. He calls God the one "who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Comfort received becomes comfort passed on. The Catholic priest Henri Nouwen wrote a whole book called The Wounded Healer, about how a minister's own loneliness and pain can become a place where others find welcome. Third, the room down the hall. Some recovery groups are built on it: a person who has been through it, sitting with a person going through it. Some hospitals and clinics bring in peer supporters, people with lived experience of an illness, to sit beside those newly facing it. Nobody has to explain what the first night feels like. Fourth, a caution. Nobody owes their wound to anyone, and some wounds are still too open to lend out. One way to put it: help from a scar, not from a fresh cut. On some days, you are the one who needs the soup. On others, what you came through may be what someone else needs to hear.

segments.voice: Let one hard thing you've come through come to mind, one that has begun to heal, not one still raw, and ask quietly what you learned there that someone else might need: a phone number, a sentence that helped, something nobody told you at the start. Then hold in mind one person near the beginning of something like it, and what you might offer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Chiron, the wounded centaur of Greek myth whose own hurt never closes, and who still teaches healing to others. Today's word.
Your line: the wound helps. What you came through may light the way for someone just starting out. See you tomorrow.

746.title: Not punishment
746.hook: Job's friends were wrong: suffering isn't proof you've failed
746.howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job, Luke 13:1–5 and Ecclesiastes 9:11 when someone asks whether a disaster was deserved, and some pastoral counselors use these texts to gently challenge the idea that suffering is proof of guilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Chiron. Your line was the wound helps, from a scar, not a fresh cut.

Some people arrive with terrible news. Pilate has killed a group of Galileans while they were offering their sacrifices. Their blood is mixed with the blood of the animals. In Luke's Gospel, the people tell this to Jesus, and a question hangs in the air that nobody says out loud. He says it for them: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?" It's an old question, and it comes up after a diagnosis, a layoff, a crash. What did they do to deserve it? What did I?
screen: `TERRIBLE NEWS FROM GALILEE.` → `THE QUESTION NOBODY SAYS.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: First, the old equation. Suffer, and you must have done something. It's the logic of Job's friends. Eliphaz asks Job to name one innocent person who ever perished, as if the answer settled things. At the end of the book, God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has. The book of Job doesn't explain suffering. But it does refuse the equation. Second, the answer in Luke. Jesus answers his own question: "I tell you, Nay." Then he raises a second disaster, one with no villain at all: "those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" And again: "I tell you, Nay." Third, the hard line after it. Jesus goes on: "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Readers take that in different ways. Some hear it as a call to everyone listening to turn to God, because life is short and nobody is safe. Others hear a warning about the coming troubles of that time. What it doesn't do is say the eighteen earned the tower. Fourth, time and chance. Ecclesiastes, a book of the Hebrew Bible, puts it plainly: "time and chance happeneth to them all." Towers fall. Cells divide wrong. Companies close. Some suffering has causes we can name and change, and that's worth knowing. But in these texts, a hard thing landing on someone is not, by itself, a verdict on that someone. That holds for the people on the news, and it holds closer to home.
screen: `THE OLD EQUATION.` · `I TELL YOU, NAY.` · `THE HARD LINE AFTER IT.` · `TIME AND CHANCE.` · then, large: `NOT PUNISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Is there something hard in your life you've quietly filed under my fault, or what I deserve? Not a real mistake you might want to make right, but a story that says the suffering itself proves something bad about you. Hold it lightly, then on an out-breath set it down like a heavy bag at the door, and breathe without it; if you pray, you can hand it to God.
Not punishment: from Job to the tower of Siloam, suffering is not, by itself, proof that someone failed. Today's word.
Your line: I tell you, nay. Towers fall, and time and chance happen to all. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Not numb
747.hook: how to hold the world's suffering, war and hunger, without going numb
747.howItsDone: Some people keep a small, regular gift for one distant cause, so hard news has somewhere to go; others hold a named place in prayer, or write to someone in a position to help.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not punishment: pain isn't, by itself, proof of failure.

Eleven at night. A phone lights up on the nightstand. A headline about a war. Under it, a photo of a line of people waiting for bread. A thumb hovers for a second. Then it keeps moving: a recipe, a joke, a friend's new haircut. Nobody in that moment is cruel. The heart has simply been asked to hold more than one heart can hold, and it closes the door a little. In everyday speech, that closing is called going numb. Two old voices speak to keeping the door open without being flattened by what comes through.
screen: `A HEADLINE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THE THUMB KEEPS MOVING.` → `THE DOOR CLOSES A LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the Chinese teacher Mencius. In one passage he asks his listeners to imagine a person who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and pity. Not to win the parents' favor, not to be praised, not because the child's crying is annoying. Just that jolt. Mencius calls that feeling a beginning of kindness, and some readers picture it as a sprout, the first shoot of a plant. A sprout is small, and it can be trampled. It can also be tended. Second, what numbness is. Read with Mencius in mind, it isn't proof that someone has no heart. It can be a sprout that got too much weather at once. The feeling doesn't die; it goes under, because it had nowhere to go. Third, a voice from Jewish tradition. In the Mishnah, in the collection called the Sayings of the Fathers, Rabbi Tarfon says something like this: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, both needed. The first half lifts the weight: no one person ends a war or a famine. The second half keeps the door open: walking away entirely isn't the answer either. Fourth, the two together, each in its own place: Mencius says the feeling is a beginning; Tarfon says do your part without needing to finish the whole. The feeling stays alive when it is given one small thing to do. A gift, a letter, learning a place's name and where it is on the map. Not everything. One thing.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.` · `NUMB IS A SPROUT UNDER TOO MUCH WEATHER.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT FREE TO LEAVE.` · `GIVE THE FEELING ONE THING TO DO.` · then, large: `NOT NUMB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where people are suffering now, say its name quietly, and notice whatever comes, a jolt, a tiredness, or nothing; any of it is fine. Then choose one small act for that place: a gift, a message to someone who can help, one honest account read from there. If you pray, you can hold that place in prayer.
Not numb: keeping the heart's first jolt alive by giving it one small thing to do, without needing to finish the whole work. Today's word.
Your line: a beginning of kindness. One act is enough for today. That's day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: One day at a time
748.hook: Jesus: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof (Matthew 6:34)
748.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer each morning, asking for 'this day our daily bread', and turn to Matthew 6 in anxious seasons; recovery groups use the phrase 'one day at a time' in a similar spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not numb: a child at the edge of a well, and work you don't have to finish. Your line was a beginning of kindness.

"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It sounds like something carved over an old courthouse door. It's actually the last line of a short talk about worry in the Gospel of Matthew, and in the story Jesus says it to a crowd on a hillside. The text calls them the multitudes: people with bills, harvests and children of their own to worry about. He doesn't tell them their troubles are imaginary. He tells them something stranger. Today has enough of its own.
screen: `A LINE THAT SOUNDS LIKE A COURTHOUSE.` → `A CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.` → `TODAY HAS ENOUGH OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the King James Bible the passage keeps saying "take no thought." Readers sometimes hear that as don't plan. The talk is about worry, the kind that runs ahead and chews on things that haven't happened. Second, the birds and the flowers. "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them." And then: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." In between, a question with a smile in it: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" Worry, it turns out, doesn't make anyone taller. Third, the closing line in full. "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Evil here means trouble, hardship. Notice what the line admits. Today has trouble. It doesn't promise an easy day. It says one day's share is enough to carry, and tomorrow's share can wait for tomorrow. Fourth, where it sits. The same sermon, a little earlier, holds the prayer Christians call the Lord's Prayer, with its line "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread for this day. Not a year's supply. Some readers hear the two together: trust practiced one day at a time. And the same shape turns up outside the church too, in recovery rooms and hospital waiting rooms: handle today. Just today.

749.title: Tisha B'Av
749.hook: on the ninth of Av, Jews mourn the destruction of the Temples and read Lamentations
749.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, observant Jews fast, sit low as mourners do, and hear Lamentations (Eikhah) chanted in the synagogue; the plea 'renew our days as of old' is repeated at the end of the reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Jesus; your line, today is enough. That closes a week of practices for hard days.
screen: `TODAY IS ENOUGH.` · `A WEEK OF PRACTICES FOR HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: A summer evening. In a synagogue the lights are low. Some people are sitting on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at a shiva. Nobody greets each other with the usual warmth. Someone begins to read from a short book of poems, in a slow, falling chant. On this one day of the year, a whole community sits like a family at a funeral, for a loss that happened long before anyone in the room was born. The day is called Tisha B'Av.
screen: `LIGHTS LOW, PEOPLE ON THE FLOOR.` → `A SLOW, FALLING CHANT.` → `A FUNERAL FOR A CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the date. Tisha B'Av is the ninth of the Jewish month of Av. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish teaching, lists the calamities tradition remembers on that day, among them the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, the first time and the second. It is kept as a fast. Second, the book. The reading is Lamentations, short poems of grief for Jerusalem. A few days ago, this path heard a turn in its third chapter; this reading starts at the beginning. Its Hebrew name is its first word, Eikhah: how. In the King James Bible it opens, "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Your line today says it in plain modern words: how lonely sits the city. Third, the picture. The poet doesn't describe rubble. The city becomes a woman sitting alone, a widow, weeping in the night with no one to comfort her. Grief that is too big for a list of facts gets a body and a face. That may be why the book still works: a person can sit beside a person. Fourth, the ending. The last chapter turns to a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Then one more verse, bitter, about being rejected. In the synagogue, the custom is to repeat the plea for renewal after it, so the reading does not end in the dark. Nothing is fixed. Nobody pretends the loss didn't happen. But the community grieves out loud, together, on a set day, and then rises from the floor.
screen: `THE NINTH OF AV, A DAY OF FASTING.` · `EIKHAH: HOW.` · `THE CITY AS A WIDOW.` · `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.` · then, large: `HOW LONELY SITS THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Read the opening verse once more, slowly, and let it stand for whatever it stands for today: a place you lost, a home that changed, a loss people around you carry, or simply a people who have read these words in grief for a very long time. No need to fix anything; sit beside it.
Tisha B'Av: the ninth of Av, the Jewish day of mourning for the Temples, when Lamentations is read low and slow. Today's word.
Your line: how lonely sits the city. Grief can have a set day, a set place, and company. See you tomorrow.
